title: Was the Home Strange to You, or Did You Disown Its Inhabitant?
intro: Ihab al-Shabatat addresses the people of Palestine in this poem, recorded by Khalid al-Sharafi and released by Alqimmah Studio in January 2024. A keffiyeh speaks for someone who has no voice, while a man who can speak promises to work wonders through normalisation. When the poet turns to the dead, public argument gives way to the grief of one man who has run out of tears.

translation: Was the home strange to you, or did you disown its inhabitant?
Palestine has never denied even a tenth of the truth.
1.sharh: The opening moves from a home to the person in it. The near-identical sound of the Arabic words for failing to recognise and pretending not to know makes the listener answer for the difference.

translation: To her a blind man walked when he wished to see
truth with an eye that had never seen light.
2.sharh: The blind man's journey turns sight into an act of understanding. He goes to this particular place to recognise something a lifetime of eyesight might have missed.

translation: Deaf men stood bewildered there, hearing
from the mouth of truth words sweet as a pipe to the ear.
3.sharh: Truth now has a mouth as well as a sound. Astonishment belongs to those who can hear this music despite their deafness.

translation: Those without speech took to wearing the keffiyeh when
they meant to say, “Here are men, and free ones.”
4.sharh: The headcloth makes a public statement about freedom without its wearer saying a word. It is the third means of recognition after sight and hearing.

translation: By my life, the speechless speak more clearly than a mouth
that says, “With normalisation we will work wonders.”
5.sharh: The keffiyeh has already spoken for its wearer. The boast makes normalisation sound like a feat of magic. The same Arabic plural can also mean the hours before dawn, holding out the promise of a new day.

translation: If people could choose their own descent,
Palestine would be the ancestry they sought as their lot.
6.sharh: Descent usually comes to a person unbidden. Given the choice, the speaker imagines people claiming kinship with Palestine as something to be desired.

translation: You overcame the lies of denial, wondrous in your endurance,
until unbelief itself called on the All-Prevailing by name.
7.sharh: Their endurance makes denial unsustainable. Even unbelief is imagined invoking God as al-Qahhar, “the All-Prevailing”, with the letter that marks the definite name in Arabic.

translation: They thought of you as Yankees thought of “their Indians”.
Such assumptions about Palestine were a burden of guilt.
8.sharh: The possessive in “their Indians” belongs to the presumption under attack. He hears in it the same assumption that another people's future can be disposed of from outside.

translation: Good intentions went to sleep on their tongues,
while secret malice in their hearts kept vigil all night.
9.sharh: Professed goodwill falls asleep where it was uttered. Malice does the work of a night watchman inside those very same speakers.

translation: Tell those who have woven such intricate plots
that Palestine has undone no button of her glory.
10.sharh: Schemes have been woven like cloth. The image continues when glory becomes the garment that Palestine keeps fastened, down to its buttons.

translation: Do not blame a lion for a pack of hyenas' treachery
when he found no fellow lions to come to his aid.
11.sharh: A lone lion faces the hyenas. His isolation brings the other lions into the picture through their absence when he needed help.

translation: My Lord appointed Job a sign of patience,
and in you today his gifts are seen anew.
12.sharh: Job supplied the example of endurance through affliction. The people he addresses allow him to recognise a divine gift of that kind again in his own time.

translation: By God's leave Jesus restored precious lives,
and you are a messiah who put our shame to death.
13.sharh: Jesus gives life, while the people likened to him put something to death. The reversal turns on what dies here, the shame the living had borne.

translation: History favoured you with every precious thing.
Called to account, it counted a thousand years and reasons.
14.sharh: History is a giver obliged to justify its apparent favouritism. It has a thousand years to draw upon for its defence.

translation: I stood against it as judge and witness,
and learnt that such beauty had never deceived.
15.sharh: He gives himself three awkward parts in the trial, opponent, judge and witness. Even from those different positions he finds no deception in the beauty history has shown him.

translation: Your forearms spoke, and some people thought
a generous arm could produce ideas.
16.sharh: An arm speaks by what it does. The astonished listeners take that figure of speech so seriously that they credit the forearm itself with thought.

translation: I told them, “You are right. What they scatter I
gather up, and among people I call it poetry.”
17.sharh: He claims the modest part of someone picking up what others have scattered. The word for scattering also means prose, so what he collects changes form when he calls it poetry.

translation: If you come to the aid of my tongue, long before now
you rallied to aid Islam and the Arabs for generations.
18.sharh: They have already helped him find words by giving him something worth saying. The same root for coming to someone's aid carries that debt back over generations.

translation: Your deeds weigh exactly as much as your words.
For all its metre, my verse can add no weight.
19.sharh: Weight first measures the match between deeds and words. In poetry the same Arabic word means metre, something his lines possess even when they can add nothing to the deeds.

translation: Eat a free man's harvest and fast from slaves' fare.
Rain comes from the high clouds, never from the valleys.
20.sharh: Fruit must be taken from its source. The valley may fill with water, but it is the high cloud that gives the rain, his image for the giver's freedom.

translation: If enemies have bloodied the dark earth of your land,
they have dyed my heart black with grief.
21.sharh: The dark soil and the heart take on colours together. Blood shed on the ground leaves a black stain in someone far away.

translation: The heart's rancour is curse enough against them,
after a lifetime of depression and changing fortunes.
22.sharh: The heart need only bring its own history of distress as a curse against those who caused it. It has a whole lifetime behind the feeling.

translation: Had the love of my youth not dried up my tears,
you would have seen their dew fill cups, then rivers.
23.sharh: Youthful love used up the water he needs for this grief. His imagined tears start as dew, then rise past the measure of cups to that of rivers.

translation: Now when my eyes can shed no more tears
they call to my heart, “Send me blood in streams.”
24.sharh: The eyes and heart become two speakers. Once tears fail, the eyes ask the heart to supply the one liquid it can give.

translation: Noble blood never disgraced a free man's land. From
a martyr's blood the earth sends up flowers.
25.sharh: The word for free or noble belongs first to the person and then to the blood. The sentence pauses on “from” before revealing what the flowers draw on.

translation: My God's peace upon every martyred soul.
Remembering our parting has made my heart ache.
26.sharh: The public argument gives way to a greeting. He sends it to each soul singly, then addresses the absent together as their loss comes back to him.

translation: May God clothe your bones in the garments of paradise.
What perfumes, by God, they became deep in the earth.
27.sharh: The bones are first dressed, then imagined dissolving into fragrances in the ground. Scent allows what is buried and unseen to be felt among the living.

translation: Memories of you fill our breasts with moonlight,
and it consoles us when the heart remembers moons.
28.sharh: Moonlight starts as something a memory gives off. By the second half the dead themselves are the moons, whose return to mind offers consolation.

translation: If longing had flesh and a beating heart,
it would beat its wings with yearning and take flight as birds.
29.sharh: He gives longing flesh so that it can have a heartbeat. A beat is also what a wing makes, and by the end there are birds in the air.

translation: By God, no breeze ever brushed our nostrils
without bringing word of you in rustling sound and scent.
30.sharh: The breeze is a messenger with no need of words. It makes the absent known in two different ways, a faint sound and a fragrance.

translation: If lives could be ransomed with poetry,
I would bring its rhymes, even if the measure held azfar.
31.sharh: He would hand over his rhymes as payment if words could bring back the dead. What fills the measure remains open. Azfar can mean nails or claws, or a nail-shaped incense that recalls the fragrance in the preceding verse.

translation: I have left your souls in my Lord's keeping.
They see other sights than I see as I lie awake at night.
32.sharh: He entrusts the souls to God. His own wakeful eye can imagine their different vision but cannot share it.

translation: Among the world's miseries is that a man should see
someone of unclean hand washing the already pure for prayer.
33.sharh: Ritual washing ought to prepare a person for prayer. Here the hand that claims authority to wash others is itself unclean, while those it touches are already pure.

translation: Alas that madness should come to please a man of sense.
Alas that he should meet death by choice.
34.sharh: The repeated cry of grief marks two inversions, reason welcoming madness and a person willingly meeting death. Both follow the spectacle of an impure hand claiming to purify others.

translation: No grief for a world that shows good to the wicked.
No grief for a world that shows evil to the good.
35.sharh: He has mourned the people who suffer these reversals. The world that deals out good and evil so perversely receives the same refrain with the lament turned off.

1.1.4.head: تَناكَرَ
1.1.4.meaning: To act as though someone were a stranger, to disown an acquaintance.

1.1.5.head: دَيّار
1.1.5.meaning: An inhabitant or a single soul, in a turn of phrase often used of an empty house.

1.2.1.head: فِلَسطين
1.2.1.meaning: Palestine, addressed both as a land and as the people who live there.

1.2.6.head: مِعشار
1.2.6.meaning: A tenth, hence even a small portion.

3.2.6.head: مِزمار
3.2.6.meaning: A wind instrument, here the pipe whose music the words resemble.

4.1.4.head: كوفِيَّة
4.1.4.meaning: Keffiyeh, a headcloth that has become a widely recognised sign of Palestinian identity.

5.2.2.head: تَطبيع
5.2.2.meaning: Normalisation, the political term here for establishing ordinary relations with Israel.

5.2.4.head: أَسحار
5.2.4.meaning: Spells or feats of magic. The same plural also denotes the hours just before dawn.

6.2.3.head: الطَّليبَة
6.2.3.meaning: One sought after, here the ancestry a person would seek.

7.1.4.head: نُكر
7.1.4.meaning: Something astonishing or beyond ordinary experience.

7.2.5.head: قَهّار
7.2.5.meaning: Al-Qahhar, the All-Prevailing, one of the divine names. The poet repeats the q sound of “you overcame” in the first half. The initial consonant can be hard to distinguish in this recording.

8.1.3.head: اليانِكي
8.1.3.meaning: Yankee, identified on the studio card here with white settlers and colonisers in North America.

8.1.5.head: هُنود
8.1.5.meaning: “Their Indians” reproduces the possessive colonial expression invoked in the comparison.

8.2.5.head: أَوزار
8.2.5.meaning: Burdens, especially guilty burdens one must answer for.

9.1.5.head: لُسن
9.1.5.meaning: Tongues, hence spoken professions of goodwill.

9.2.1.head: أَخباث
9.2.1.meaning: Vile things, here the hidden promptings of the heart.

10.1.5.head: دَسائِس
10.1.5.meaning: Schemes or intrigues laid in secret.

11.1.6.head: أَضبُع
11.1.6.meaning: Hyenas. A group of them is set against a single lion.

11.2.6.head: الأُسد
11.2.6.meaning: Lions, in the plural. The solitary animal looks to its own kind.

12.1.3.head: أَيّوب
12.1.3.meaning: Job, the prophet commended for patience during affliction in Quran 38.41–44.

12.2.3.head: آلاء
12.2.3.meaning: Blessings or favours bestowed by God.

13.1.1.head: عيسى
13.1.1.meaning: Jesus son of Mary. In Quran 3.49 he gives life to the dead by God's leave.

13.2.2.head: مَسيح
13.2.2.meaning: Masih, the Messiah, a title of Jesus. The studio also notes its use of a handsome face.

14.1.1.head: حابى
14.1.1.meaning: To favour someone with gifts or preference.

14.2.1.head: ليمَ
14.2.1.meaning: Was blamed or called to account. History is the one put on trial.

15.2.6.head: غَرّار
15.2.6.meaning: Deceptive, liable to beguile the beholder.

16.1.1.head: زُنود
16.1.1.meaning: Forearms or wrists, standing for what people accomplish with their hands.

17.2.1.head: لَمَّ
17.2.1.meaning: I gather up what has been scattered.

18.2.1.head: تَناجَدَ
18.2.1.meaning: To rally together to give help.

19.1.4.head: وَزن
19.1.4.meaning: Weight on a scale. The same Arabic word also names the metre of a poem.

20.1.3.meaning: Fruit gathered or ready for picking.

20.2.6.meaning: To bring rain and the relief it gives.

22.1.4.head: دَعو
22.1.4.meaning: An invocation, here a curse called down upon someone.

23.1.6.meaning: Youth, particularly the time of youthful loves.

24.2.6.head: مِدرار
24.2.6.meaning: Flowing in abundance, in one stream after another.

25.1.2.meaning: To mar, disfigure, or bring into disrepute.

25.1.5-6.head: حُرُّ دَم
25.1.5-6.meaning: “Noble blood” transfers the quality of the free person to what has been shed.

27.1.5.head: الجِنان
27.1.5.meaning: The gardens of paradise in the life to come.

27.2.4-5.head: حَشا التُّرب
27.2.4-5.meaning: “The belly of the soil” is the earth's interior where the dead lie.

29.1.5.head: خافِق
29.1.5.meaning: A beating heart. The verb also describes the beat of a wing.

30.2.4.head: هَفيف
30.2.4.meaning: A soft rustle or whisper of moving air.

31.1.5.head: اِفتَدى
31.1.5.meaning: To be redeemed for a ransom.

31.2.4.meaning: To measure something out, as in a transaction.

31.2.5.head: أَظفار
31.2.5.meaning: Azfar, nails or claws. The same word names nail-shaped pieces of incense. Either sense can belong to what is measured out here.

32.1.1.head: ذِمَّة
32.1.1.meaning: A pledge of protection or safe keeping.

33.2.1.head: نَجيس
33.2.1.meaning: Deeply unclean, used of a person claiming the authority to purify others.

33.2.4.head: وَضَّأَ
33.2.4.meaning: To perform the ritual washing for prayer on another person.

34.2.3.meaning: To reach or hit one's mark, here to meet death.
